content: Why does a database query sometimes stay slow after I add an index? I thought an index was a sorted copy of the whole table, so the database should find any row immediately instead of looking through everything.

An index is usually a separate structure containing selected column values plus row references, not a full sorted table copy. It helps only when the query's conditions match how that structure is organized. The database may still scan the table when many rows qualify, when the indexed column is transformed, or when reading through the index would require too many scattered row lookups.
What does it mean for the condition to match the index? If I make one index containing name, city, and age, does that give me three fast lookups, or does the order of those words matter?

For a typical B-tree index, order matters. An index on name, city, age is arranged first by name, then by city within each name, then by age. It works well for conditions beginning with name, and sometimes name plus city. A search only by age generally cannot jump to one useful region because ages are dispersed across all name and city groups.

So putting the most important box first should solve it. I assume the first box should always be the one people search most often, and then the database can use the rest whenever they happen to appear.

Frequency alone is not enough. The leading column should reflect actual query patterns and how selectively it narrows the data. Later columns can refine a matched prefix, support ordering, or let the index contain all requested values, but they are not independently searchable in the usual case. Several focused indexes can be better than one wide index, though each adds storage and write cost.

For a composite B-tree on tenant_id, status, created_at, how does the planner treat equality on tenant_id, a low-selectivity status predicate, and a created_at range? I would expect the range to terminate usable key-prefix constraints, but perhaps skip scanning changes that.

Your prefix model is right: equality on tenant_id and status can position the scan, while the range on created_at bounds it; columns after that range usually cannot further narrow the contiguous scan. Some engines implement skip scans, allowing a missing leading value to be enumerated when it has few distinct values. Whether that wins depends on cardinality estimates, clustering, cache state, and engine-specific costing.

If status has only three values, could placing created_at before status reduce the scanned range while preserving an index-supported ORDER BY created_at? How would correlation between tenant_id and status distort a planner that mostly keeps per-column statistics?

Putting created_at second can sharply bound a time-window query and naturally provide ordering within a tenant, while status becomes a residual filter unless the engine can exploit it another way. Correlated columns can make independent selectivity estimates badly wrong, causing poor scan choices. Multivariate statistics, histograms, or extended dependency statistics help, but availability and fidelity vary by engine and data distribution.

Suppose the query returns thirty percent of a tenant's rows but selects only columns present in the index. Is an index-only scan predictably preferable, or can MVCC visibility checks and leaf-page locality make a sequential or bitmap plan cheaper?

It is not predictably preferable. A genuinely covering index reduces heap access, but in MVCC systems such as PostgreSQL, index entries do not always prove tuple visibility; insufficiently all-visible heap pages still require checks. A large result fraction also increases leaf reads and CPU work. Good clustering may favor a regular index scan, bitmap access may batch heap pages, and a sequential scan can win when most relevant pages must be touched anyway.

Would adding an index to every column make a database generally faster? I believe indexes are just extra shortcuts, so apart from using more disk space, there should not be much reason to leave any column without one.

Indexes speed some reads, but they impose work on every insert, delete, and relevant update. The database must maintain each structure, write more log data, and keep additional pages in memory. Many single-column indexes also may not match real multi-column filters or sorting needs. A useful index starts from an important query pattern, not merely from the existence of a column.

Why would changing one row touch several of these shortcuts? If I update only the phone number, I would expect the database to replace that one value and leave indexes on email, date, and customer number completely alone.

The exact behavior depends on the engine. The phone index certainly needs a new entry or an in-place change. Other indexes may still be affected because some systems create a new row version when updating, and their index entries identify that version. Engines have optimizations that avoid rewriting unchanged indexes in favorable cases, but page space, indexed columns, and concurrency rules determine whether those optimizations apply.

Then it seems safest to remove all the shortcuts from tables that receive lots of new orders. Writes are the important part there, and searches can probably just check the rows afterward without causing a serious problem.

Removing every index usually swings too far. Order creation still needs constraint checks, lookups, status processing, and joins; without suitable indexes, those operations can scan growing tables or hold locks longer. Keep the smallest set that supports critical reads and integrity constraints. Measure write latency and query plans, because one well-chosen composite or partial index may replace several less useful ones.

In PostgreSQL, an update can remain HOT only when no indexed column changes and the target heap page has room. For an append-heavy orders table with occasional status transitions, how should fillfactor be balanced against cache density and the write amplification from status indexes?

A lower fillfactor reserves page space for new tuple versions, increasing the chance of HOT updates, but expands the heap and reduces cache density. If status is indexed, status transitions cannot be HOT regardless of free space, so lowering fillfactor helps only other updates. Measure transition frequency separately from inserts, consider moving mutable status to a narrower companion table, and compare WAL volume, heap growth, and read latency under representative load.

A partial index on pending rows might avoid maintaining entries after completion, though each transition still deletes an old entry. Could predicate churn or generic prepared plans erase that advantage, especially when the planner cannot prove that a parameter implies the partial-index predicate?

Yes. The partial index stays small and excludes completed inserts, but each row leaving the predicate creates cleanup work and dead index entries until vacuum reclaims them. A generic plan often cannot assume a parameter equals the predicate's constant, so it may reject the partial index. Custom plans, literalized statements, or separate query paths can help, with a trade-off in planning overhead and statement management.

For sustained ingestion, would a BRIN index on monotonically increasing created_at be a better complement than another B-tree? I suspect the crossover depends on physical correlation and range width, but how should autosummarization lag and late-arriving records enter the decision?

That is the right uncertainty. BRIN is tiny and cheap to maintain when created_at correlates strongly with heap order and queries cover meaningful time ranges. Unsummarized page ranges can temporarily reduce pruning, so autosummarization cadence matters. Late arrivals widen stored min-max bounds for older ranges and can create false positives; modest disorder is often acceptable, while heavy backfilling may justify smaller pages-per-range, explicit summarization, or a B-tree for narrow probes.

What makes a database ignore an index even when the searched column has one? I think the planner sometimes picks randomly, because the same kind of filter can be quick one day and scan every row another day.

The planner estimates the cost of available strategies rather than choosing randomly. Its decision depends on how many rows it expects, data distribution statistics, table size, cached pages, and the form of the condition. Different parameter values or changed statistics can produce different plans. A scan is often deliberate when many rows match, though stale estimates can make that decision wrong.

Why does wrapping a field in something simple matter? If I ask for LOWER(email) to equal a lowercase address, the index still contains the same letters, so it seems obvious that the database can search it normally.

A normal index is ordered by the original email values, not by the results of applying LOWER. The transformed values may have a different ordering, so the engine cannot generally jump to the matching region. A functional index on LOWER(email), or a case-insensitive data type or collation where appropriate, gives it a searchable structure matching the expression. Exact syntax and behavior vary among databases.

Then a text index should fix all searches with percent signs too. I assume the database can skip through the index letters for both 'alex%' and '%alex', since both patterns contain the same useful word.

A B-tree can usually support 'alex%' because the known prefix corresponds to a contiguous alphabetical range. With '%alex', the unknown beginning allows matches anywhere, so there is no single range to seek. Suffix searches may use an index on reversed text; arbitrary substring searches are better served by trigram, full-text, or specialized inverted indexes, depending on the desired matching semantics.

More precisely, prefix sargability also depends on operator class and collation. Under a nondeterministic ICU collation, can a B-tree safely derive LIKE bounds, or would a pattern-operations index require a deterministic bytewise ordering that changes equality semantics?

Correct: collation semantics can prevent safe range derivation. Pattern operator classes commonly impose a deterministic character or byte-oriented ordering suitable for prefix bounds, while ordinary equality and ordering may follow the column's locale collation. A separate pattern index can therefore accelerate LIKE without replacing the semantic index. Nondeterministic collations and feature support differ across engine versions, so the exact permissible combinations must be checked for the target system.

For parameterized predicates, when does plan caching become the larger problem than sargability? A skewed tenant_id distribution seems liable to make one generic selectivity estimate alternate between an efficient index scan for small tenants and a poor plan for dominant tenants.

That is a classic parameter-sensitivity problem. A custom plan can use the bound tenant's estimated frequency, whereas a generic plan averages away the skew. Generic planning saves repeated optimization time but can choose badly at either extreme. Remedies include extended statistics, filtered or partitioned designs, forcing custom plans selectively, or splitting query paths for dominant tenants. The best choice depends on execution frequency, planning cost, and skew stability.

How robust are expression indexes when the indexed function is marked immutable but depends indirectly on collation rules or an extension version? I would expect upgrades to risk semantic drift even if the planner continues matching the expression tree exactly.

Expression matching and stored-value correctness are separate issues. The planner may recognize the same expression while previously indexed results no longer agree with revised collation or extension behavior. Databases can track some collation-version changes and warn that affected objects need rebuilding, but indirect dependencies are not always visible. Treat immutability as a contract, audit upgrade notes, and REINDEX whenever a dependency can alter computed keys or their ordering.

Is the primary-key index what keeps related rows next to each other on disk? I believe customer orders with nearby numbers are stored together automatically, which is why reading the next page of results should always be fast.

Not in every database. Some engines organize table rows by the primary key, while others keep a separate heap and use the primary-key index to point into it. Even in a clustered organization, page splits, deletions, and inserted key patterns affect locality. Reading the next result page can also be slow if the query must skip many earlier rows or fetch unindexed columns elsewhere.
What is the difference between the main key shortcut and an index on customer name, then? If both point to rows, I do not see why one would care where the row itself happens to sit.

In a heap-organized table, both may ultimately locate heap rows, although uniqueness and storage details differ. In a clustered engine such as InnoDB, the primary-key B-tree contains the row data, while a secondary index usually stores its own key plus the primary-key value. Fetching columns absent from that secondary index then requires another lookup into the clustered tree, making row placement and key width important.

So selecting only the name should always be instant if name has an index, and adding every displayed column to that shortcut sounds strictly better. Then the database never needs to visit the real row at all.

A covering index can avoid a separate row lookup, but 'instant' is too strong. It may still scan many index entries, check visibility, sort, or read pages from storage. Adding displayed columns enlarges the index, reduces fan-out, consumes cache, and increases write work. Include columns are useful for stable, frequent queries, but a very wide covering index can cost more overall than occasional row fetches.

In InnoDB terms, my earlier assumption only applies to the clustered primary-key tree; secondary leaves carry the primary key rather than a physical row pointer. For a wide UUID primary key, how severe is the multiplicative cost across secondary indexes?

It can be substantial because every secondary leaf entry repeats the full primary key, increasing index size, memory pressure, I/O, and split frequency. Random UUID insertion also scatters writes in the clustered tree unless the UUID layout is time-ordered. The impact scales with row count and number of secondary indexes. A narrow surrogate key reduces amplification, though it introduces another uniqueness index if the UUID remains a business identifier.

For pagination on created_at, id, keyset predicates avoid OFFSET work, but concurrent inserts and nonunique timestamps complicate boundaries. Under READ COMMITTED, can a lexicographic continuation condition guarantee neither duplicates nor omissions without holding a snapshot across requests?

No. The composite boundary makes traversal deterministic for a fixed snapshot, but separate READ COMMITTED requests can see different committed sets. Inserts before the saved boundary may be omitted, while updates to ordering keys can move rows across it and cause omissions or repeats. Holding a consistent snapshot, using an immutable high-water mark, or accepting documented weak consistency are the usual choices; each trades freshness against stability and operational cost.

Would including a monotonically assigned sequence as the final tie-breaker solve only total ordering, not snapshot drift? I suspect a high-water predicate sequence <= initial_max helps inserts, while updates to created_at still require immutability or versioned rows.

Exactly. The sequence gives a unique total order and an initial maximum excludes later inserts, but neither prevents existing rows from changing position when created_at is mutable. Making ordering columns immutable is simplest. Otherwise, paginate over versioned records or materialize the result set. Deletions can still shorten later pages, though they do not create duplicates; strict repeatability ultimately requires snapshot-like state somewhere.
